rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some Muslims' attachment to Quraysh kin remained hidden until war against the idolaters was commanded; then their hesitation and efforts to placate Quraysh leaders exposed it.
rows.anchor: once the Muslims were asked to go after the idolaters, this weakness started to become evident.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi regards this as accommodation for a favorable expediency, rather than hypocrisy: they hoped friendly relations might bring their relatives to Islam.
rows.anchor: This attitude of these Muslims was more akin to conciliation with the circumstances, than to hypocrisy;

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an condemns the compromise as contrary to faith, which requires severing relations with those who are enemies of God and the believers.
rows.anchor: the Qur’ ān regarded this compromise as being against the dictates of faith.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word for enemy can denote either singular or plural entities.
rows.anchor: used for both singular and plural entities.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse explains that Muslims were extending friendly ties to idolaters who were God's and the Muslims' enemies because they rejected their religion and drove them from their homes for professing faith.
rows.anchor: such Muslims have friendly ties with these idolaters while the latter are enemies of both God and the Muslims.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression suits relations often maintained by letters, and its wording recalls the warning not to cast oneself into destruction.
rows.anchor: Such relations are generally established through epistles and letters and various other means. Hence this style is very appropriate to convey this meaning.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The present tense makes the scene vivid and stirs the honor of those wishing to befriend people who expelled the Prophet and his Companions.
rows.anchor: is meant to portray the whole scenario before the eyes. It is meant to stir the honour

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God “your Lord” is argumentative: since He alone is Lord, professing faith in Him is a duty, yet this truth angers the idolaters.
rows.anchor: when God is the Lord, then He, alone, is worthy of being professed faith in.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about driving believers out for believing can be unfolded with an omitted governing noun: they are expelled on the charge of professing faith in God.
rows.anchor: At times, an ellipsis of a governing noun ( muḍāf) occurs before

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says the answer to both conditional clauses is that the person has strayed from the right path, while the statement about God's knowledge is parenthetical.
rows.anchor: Our exegetes have not been able to fully grasp the correct grammatical construction of this part. So I will firstly try to point it out.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The condition describes people going out for God's cause while hiding their wish to befriend His and His Prophet's enemies, despite God's knowledge of their inner and outer selves.
rows.anchor: If you go out for my cause for jihād and to please Me, such that you hide the desire of befriending the enemies of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fighting for God and seeking His pleasure cannot coexist with befriending His enemies, and God cannot be deceived because He knows both the inward and outward self.
rows.anchor: Both these attitudes cannot co-exist in the heart.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who go out with these contradictory intentions are effectively advancing Satan's cause rather than God's.
rows.anchor: they are, in fact, going out for the cause of Satan and not that of God.

rows.speaker: our exegetes
rows.claim: Exegetes cite an occasion of revelation involving Ḥātib ibn Abī Balta‘ah.
rows.anchor: Our exegetes have cited an occasion of revelation for this verse: it relates to a certain incident involving Ḥātib ibn Abī Balta‘ah (rta).

rows.speaker: Ḥamīd al-Dīn al-Farāhī
rows.claim: Al-Farāhī holds that an early authority's occasion-of-revelation report need not identify what caused the verse's revelation; it can show that the verse guides similar cases.
rows.anchor: my mentor Ḥamīd al-Dīn al-Farāhī in the introduction to this exegesis that when our early authorities cite an incident

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says the passage does not point to one specific incident but alludes to a general situation and a common human weakness, often hidden within sincere intentions or expediency.
rows.anchor: A little deliberation will show that it does not refer to a particular incident; it only alludes to a certain situation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone, as the all-knowing and wise, is aware of every expediency, including weaknesses that a person may conceal even from himself.
rows.anchor: knower and the wise, Who is aware of all expediencies.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The actions of the Muslim vanguard are presented as examples for later generations to follow.
rows.anchor: all the actions of the vanguard of this ummah form an example, to be followed by the later people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If hostile people overpower Muslims, they will harm them by hand or tongue and try to turn them back to their former beliefs.
rows.anchor: harming them by the hand, or even by the tongue; they will fully try to convert the Muslims back to their former beliefs.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur’an 9:8 shows their collective hostility and lack of regard for kinship or promises, so Muslims should abandon the desire to befriend them.
rows.anchor: they have no regard for any relationship or promise in this matter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Arḥām” means relationships and kinships; those who put these ties ahead of religion will gain no benefit from them on Judgment Day, when God separates such relations.
rows.anchor: connotes “relationships and kinships.” People who give preference to these ties over the requisites of religion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The separation is illustrated by the Day when even close friends do not ask after one another and sinners would offer their families and all humanity as ransom.
rows.anchor: And no friend shall inquire after his friend, [though] they shall be shown to one another.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’anic account of people fleeing their closest relatives on that Day reinforces that kinship will not protect them.
rows.anchor: On that Day, man will flee from his brother, mother and father, his wife and his sons.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur’an 9:23–24 warns believers against befriending fathers or brothers who choose disbelief and against preferring family, wealth, trade, or homes to God, His Prophet, and striving for His cause.
rows.anchor: Believers! Do not befriend your fathers or your brothers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The placement of “the Day of Judgement” makes it an adverb of place for the verbs both before and after it.
rows.anchor: it has become an adverb of place for the verbs preceding and succeeding it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that God knows what they do admonishes them that nothing they conceal escapes His knowledge.
rows.anchor: Nothing is hidden from Him; each and every deed they do is in His knowledge.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham and his companions are offered as a familiar example for Muslims to follow; the word “qad” signals that the example is already well known.
rows.anchor: their own ancestor Abraham (sws) and his companions have already set an example worthy of following for them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arabs knew traditions about Abraham's migration and sacrifice despite later obscuring and distortion, contrary to some historians' claim that they were unaware.
rows.anchor: they were aware of the traditions of his migration and sacrifice offered.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham did not migrate alone: members of his clan believed in him and migrated with him.
rows.anchor: Abraham (sws) did not migrate alone; some people of his clan, too, professed faith in him and migrated along with him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham and his companions publicly disowned their people, their deities, and their religion, declaring enmity until the people believed in the one God.
rows.anchor: They openly announced their renunciation from their people, as well as from the deities they worshipped and rejected their religion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their declared enmity followed earlier lenience to convey the message; after the message was conclusive and their people remained obstinate, the declaration called for open enmity until they accepted monotheism.
rows.anchor: their people are not left with any excuse and they are still adamant on their ill-ways

rows.speaker: our exegetes
rows.claim: Exegetes generally treat Abraham's promise to seek forgiveness for his father as an exception to the exemplary model of Abraham and his companions.
rows.anchor: Our exegetes generally think that the words

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi instead reads the promise as an exception to the declaration of renunciation, not to the exemplary model itself.
rows.anchor: in my opinion, they are an exception to the declaration of renunciation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The leniency was Abraham's promise to pray for his father's forgiveness despite having no authority over his father's matter before God.
rows.anchor: it was his promise to his father to pray for his forgiveness before God, even though, he has no authority on behalf of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's compassion and forbearance explain the leniency; he viewed praying for his father as consistent with renouncing his people and as a son's natural duty to his parents.
rows.anchor: he was very compassionate and forbearing. He thought that if he prayed for his father, then this would not be adverse to the declaration
